etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English circuler, circuleer, circulere, from Old French circulier, from Late Latin circularis, from Latin circulus, diminutive of circus (“ring”).

definitions.definition: Of or relating to a circle.
In the shape of, or moving in a circle.

quote.citation: 1918, W[illiam] B[abington] Maxwell, chapter V, in The Mirror and the Lamp, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Here, in the transept and choir, where the service was being held, one was conscious every moment of an increasing brightness; colours glowing vividly beneath the circular chandeliers, and the rows of small lights on the choristers' desks flashed and sparkled in front of the boys' faces, deep linen collars, and red neckbands.

definitions.definition: Referring back to itself, so as to prevent computation or comprehension; infinitely recursive.
Distributed to a large number of persons.

quote.citation: 1827, Henry Hallam, The Constitutional History of England from the Accession of Henry VII. to the Death of George II. […], volume (please specify |volume=I or II), London: John Murray, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: a proclamation of Henry III.,  […]  doubtless circular throughout England

quote.citation: 1632, Philip Massinger, Maid of Honour, act I, scene 2:
quote.text: A man so absolute and circular / In all those wished-for rarities that may take / A virgin captive.

definitions.definition: (archaic) Adhering to a fixed circle of legends; cyclic; hence, mean; inferior.

quote.citation: February 1, 1711, John Dennis, on the Genius and Writings of Shakespeare
quote.text: Had Virgil been a circular poet, and closely adhered to history, how could the Romans have had Dido?

definitions.definition: An advertisement, directive or notice intended for mass circulation.

quote.citation: 1991 September, Stephen Fry, chapter 2, in The Liar, London: Heinemann, →ISBN, →OCLC, section I, page 40:
quote.text: The pigeon-hole was also stuffed with circulars and hand-bills.

definitions.definition: (dated) A sleeveless cloak cut from a circular pattern.
A shuttle bus with a circular route.
To distribute circulars to or at.

quote.citation: 1851, G. W. Muir, Report on the State of Engine and Other Furnaces, page 19:
quote.text: The result of the sending of these notices confirms me in the opinion, that it will be necessary to adopt legal means with the great majority of these parties. The circulars have had little effect. In fact, the parties have been “circulared" into the notion that nothing more formidable will ever be sent to them.
It is true, that, to obtain these, some six hundred or more institutions were circulared, and a good many of these a second time.

quote.citation: 1909, American Life Convention, Report of the Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the American Life Convention, page 42:
quote.text: I do not mean to say we have never employed some of them who come to us—but we have never circulared agents or gone after them.

quote.citation: 1962, Harrie Sheridan Baketel, Medical Economics - Volume 39, page 141:
quote.text: If you've ever been circulared by drug repackaging houses, you know they usually offer to trade a selection of office supplies for your unused drug samples.

definitions.definition: To extend in a circular direction.

quote.citation: 2008, Donald E. Wagner, Kenneth Cragg, Dying in the Land of Promise, page 116:
quote.text: The theme can be expressed in an architectural analogy. For, of all contriving to encover space, the arch — alone or 'circulared' into the dome — is the most ingenious.
